# card4r

**card4r** gives R access to the
[card](https://github.com/lou-heraut/card) collection of hydroclimatic
variables: low flows, floods, seasonality, climate change, computed on
your own data.

The collection and the engine are not rewritten in R, they are
**called**. A `data.frame` goes in, `data.frame`s and their metadata
come out. Which means the numbers you get are the same ones, to the last
digit, whichever language you call them from.

## Installation

``` r

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lou-heraut/card4r")
```

There is nothing else to install. On the first call, card4r provisions
the Python environment it needs on its own (interpreter, numpy, pandas,
scipy, then `card` and `stase`), through
[reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/). Expect a few
hundred megabytes and a network connection, once. Nothing is installed
system-wide: it lives in reticulate’s cache and can be deleted at any
time, it will be rebuilt on the next call.

Each release of card4r pins the **exact versions** of card and stase it
calls, by tag rather than by branch. Two people running the same version
of card4r therefore run the same code, and
[`card_config()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_config.md)
says which:

``` r

card_config()
# python       : ~/.cache/R/reticulate/uv/cache/.../bin/python
# card         : 0.5.0
# card commit  : …
# stase        : 0.6.2
# stase commit : …
```

If you would rather supply your own Python, point at it before loading
the package and card4r will provision nothing:

``` r

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "/path/to/python")
```

That is also the way to go behind a proxy that blocks the download, or
on a machine without network access.

## Using card4r

### A first extraction

The example below runs on a real record: the Yzeron at Craponne, a
periurban catchment west of Lyon, gauged since 1970. The data comes from
[Hub’Eau](https://hubeau.eaufrance.fr/), the French open hydrological
API, which needs no key.

``` r

library(card4r)
# install.packages("jsonlite")

url <- paste0("https://hubeau.eaufrance.fr/api/v2/hydrometrie/obs_elab",
              "?code_entite=V301501001&grandeur_hydro_elab=QmnJ",
              "&date_debut_obs_elab=1970-01-01&size=20000")
obs <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)$data

data <- data.frame(date = as.Date(obs$date_obs_elab),
                   Q    = obs$resultat_obs_elab / 1000,   # Hub'Eau serves L/s
                   id   = obs$code_station)
# 19273 daily values, 1970-01-01 to 2022-10-26
```

Three columns are all card needs: a date, a series identifier, and the
numeric columns the cards ask for (`Q` for discharge, `T` for
temperature, `R` for precipitation). Then:

``` r

res <- card_extract(data, cards = c("QA", "VCN10"))

head(res$data$QA, 3)
#           id       date        QA
# 1 V301501001 1969-09-01       NaN
# 2 V301501001 1970-09-01 0.2967836
# 3 V301501001 1971-09-01 0.2786175

head(res$data$VCN10, 3)
#           id       date  VCN10
# 1 V301501001 1969-02-01    NaN
# 2 V301501001 1970-02-01 0.0155
# 3 V301501001 1971-02-01 0.0213
```

One `data.frame` per card. The first row is empty because the record
starts mid-year, and the two cards do not use the same window: `QA` runs
over the hydrological year starting in September, `VCN10` starts its
year at the month of highest flows, February here.

These are the same values, digit for digit, as the Python example in
[card’s README](https://github.com/lou-heraut/card#a-first-extraction).
That is the whole point of the package: one definition, one engine, two
languages.

Alongside the values, `res$meta` holds one row per variable produced:

``` r

res$meta[, c("variable_en", "unit_en", "name_en", "version")]
#   variable_en      unit_en                                      name_en version
# 1          QA m^{3}.s^{-1}                  Annual mean daily discharge     1.0
# 2       VCN10 m^{3}.s^{-1} Annual minimum of 10-day mean daily discharge     1.1
```

It also carries the description, the classification, the method step by
step and both languages, plus what it takes to trace the computation,
which the last section of this part covers.

### Finding your variable

The whole collection is browsable online: **[the
catalogue](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card/CARDS)**, and [in
French](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card/CARDS.fr). From R:

``` r

card_list()                          # every variable, one per row
card_list(phenomenon = "low flows")  # by hydrological phenomenon
card_list(output = "series")         # a series, versus a scalar or a curve
card_list(operator = "delta")        # the change between two periods
card_info("VCN10", lang = "en")      # one card, drawn
```

Facets accept English as well as French (`output = "series"` or
`output = "série"`).

Card names are systematic and can be read rather than looked up: `QJXA`
is discharge, daily, maximum, annual. The grammar is summarised at the
top of the [catalogue](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card/CARDS) and
given in full in
[NOMENCLATURE.md](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card/dev/NOMENCLATURE).

### Trend

``` r

tr <- card_trend(res)

tr$data$VCN10[, c("id", "h", "p", "a", "a_relative")]
#           id    h          p             a a_relative
# 1 V301501001 TRUE 0.05671581 -0.0001151515  -1.069519
```

The low flows of this catchment decline by about **1.1 % per year** over
the record. `h` says whether the trend is significant at the requested
level, `0.1` by default, `a` is the Sen slope in the unit of the
variable per year, and `a_relative` the same as a percentage of the
mean.

[`card_trend()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_trend.md)
takes the object
[`card_extract()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_extract.md)
returned, and not a table you rebuilt yourself: it needs the time column
as card handed it over, before card4r turned it into `Date` for you.

### What a result says about itself

``` r

res$meta[1, c("version", "swhid", "card_commit", "stase_commit")]
#   version                swhid card_commit stase_commit
# 1     1.0 swh:1:cnt:e1197d4d…           …            …
```

`version` is that of the **card**, which changes as soon as its outputs
change, and `swhid` identifies the card file itself in [Software
Heritage](https://archive.softwareheritage.org/). The two commits
identify the **software** that ran: a version number designates a unique
state only on the day it is published, a commit always does.

An exported result therefore says what produced it, which is what it
takes to cite it or to replay it years later.
[`card_config()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_config.md)
prints the same without running a computation.

## What card4r does not do, and will not do

- **Write a card in R.** A card is a YAML file of the collection, and
  that is what keeps a single definition for both languages. Writing or
  contributing one happens in
  [card](https://github.com/lou-heraut/card#writing-your-own), and the
  card you write there is immediately usable from here.
- **Re-export the hydrological functions** (`compute_FDC`, `get_BFI`…).
  They remain the internal machinery of the cards.

These two limits are not gaps: they are what keeps the package a bridge
instead of a second engine to maintain. The day a function had to cross
the bridge, the cost would go from a weekend to a year.

## Coming from the CARD package

[CARD](https://github.com/lou-heraut/CARD-R) is the original R package,
where card comes from. It still installs and is not going away, but it
is no longer developed: the living version is on the card side.

Switching does not change your results. **Checked on 2026-08-05, values
from `card4r` and from `CARD` match to 1.8e-15**, machine precision, and
that comparison runs with this package’s test suite.

| CARD (R) | card4r |
|----|----|
| `CARD_extraction(data, CARD_name = ...)` | `card_extract(data, cards = ...)` |
| `CARD_list_all()` | [`card_list()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_list.md) |
| `CARD_management(...)` | `card_info(...)` |

The `expand_overwrite`, `rmNApct`, `rm_duplicates` and `dev` arguments
of `CARD_extraction` have no counterpart: they went away with the port.
card4r does not accept them, rather than ignore them silently.

## The ecosystem

|  |  |
|----|----|
| [card](https://github.com/lou-heraut/card) | the card collection, in Python |
| [stase](https://github.com/lou-heraut/stase) | the aggregation and trend engine |
| **card4r** | the same collection, called from R (you are here) |
| [card-api](https://github.com/lou-heraut/card-api) | the web service, on Hub’Eau discharge data |
| [CARD-R](https://github.com/lou-heraut/CARD-R) · [EXstat](https://github.com/lou-heraut/EXstat) | the historical R packages, superseded |

## Licence and citation

GPL-3. The collection, the engine and this package each have their own
`CITATION.cff`. Cite the **cards** you used, with their version, which
`res$meta` gives you.

# Package index

## Compute

A data frame goes in, data frames and their metadata come out.

- [`card_extract()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_extract.md)
  : Calculer des variables hydroclimatiques
- [`card_trend()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_trend.md)
  : Tester la stationnarité d'une extraction

## Browse the collection

Find the variable you need, then read what it is. The full catalogue is
published on the card website.

- [`card_list()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_list.md)
  : Lister les fiches du corpus
- [`card_info()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_info.md)
  : Afficher une fiche

## Know what ran

Which corpus and which engine answered, down to the commit.

- [`card_config()`](https://lou-heraut.github.io/card4r/reference/card_config.md)
  : L'environnement Python utilisé par card4r
